entry: Family of [[Beetle|beetles]], widely known as ladybugs in North America and ladybirds in Britain and Australia. The more than 6,000 described species have a global distribution. Many have conspicuous warning colors, such as red with black spots, that signal to predators that they taste bad. Most are carnivorous predators of insects such as [[Aphid|aphids]] and [[Scale insect|scale insects]], though some eat plants and fungi. Predatory species often lay eggs near prey colonies, and their [[Larva|larvae]] develop through a [[Pupa|pupa]] stage to adulthood. Several species have been introduced as biological control agents, with varying success. Some are pests themselves, and [[Invasive species|invasive species]] such as *Harmonia axyridis* can threaten native coccinellids. [[Climate change]] and habitat destruction are also threats.

Small [[Parrot|parrot]] native to [[Australia]], the only member of the genus *Nymphicus*. It is the smallest member of the [[Cockatoo|cockatoo]] family (*Cacatuidae*), known for bright orange cheek patches, long tail feathers and a sociable nature. An estimated 4.8 million U.S. households keep one, making it one of the most commonly kept companion parrots. Insufficient knowledge of its care contributes to one of the highest surrender rates among pet birds, and many are relinquished to shelters within about 1.5 years of adoption.

Any of 22 species of [[Parrot|parrots]] in the family *Cacatuidae*, native to [[Australasia]]. Cockatoos are recognizable by prominent crests and curved bills, and their plumage is generally less colorful than that of other parrots, being mainly white, gray or black. The family ranges from the [[Philippines]] and eastern Indonesian islands to [[New Guinea]], the [[Solomon Islands]] and Australia. Most species fall into two main clades: five large black cockatoos of the genus *Calyptorhynchus*, and the genus *Cacatua*, with 12 species of white-plumaged cockatoos. Cockatoos eat seeds, tubers, fruit, flowers and insects, and nest in tree hollows. Habitat loss, particularly the clearing of large mature trees that provide nest hollows, has affected some species, while others are agricultural pests. Illegal trade in wild-caught birds contributes to the decline of some species. The [[Cockatiel|cockatiel]], the smallest cockatoo, is by far the most frequently kept cockatoo in captivity.

Scarab beetle native to Europe, also known as the maybug or doodlebug. Mating is controlled by pheromones. Males swarm during the mating season and locate females through green leaf volatiles released when feeding leaves. Adults and [[Larva|larvae]] feed on plants and are agricultural pests, with larvae able to kill plants by gnawing their roots. The beetle is also an important food source for many predators. [[Carl Linnaeus|Carl Linnaeus]] first named the species in 1758 as *Scarabaeus melolontha*.

Insect of the order Blattodea, which also includes [[Termite|termites]]. About 30 of the 4,600 species are associated with human habitats, and some are well-known pests. Their ancestors, the roachoids, likely originated in the [[Carboniferous]] period around 320 million years ago, and modern cockroaches first appeared in the Late Jurassic. They have chewing mouthparts and are hardy insects that tolerate climates from [[Arctic]] cold to tropical heat. Most species are small and inoffensive, although they are popularly depicted as large, dirty pests. The gregarious [[German cockroach]] has an elaborate social structure involving common shelter, social dependence, information transfer and kin recognition. Cockroaches have appeared in human culture since [[Classical antiquity|classical antiquity]]. The irrational fear of cockroaches is called katsaridaphobia.

Mixed drink, usually [[Alcoholic beverage|alcoholic]], most commonly combining one or more spirits with other ingredients such as [[Juice|juices]], flavored syrups, tonic water and bitters. The base, usually a spirit or wine, is the most dominant ingredient and determines the style of the drink. A modifying agent, such as fruit juice, [[Cream|cream]], sugar or egg, softens the base's bite, while special flavorings such as liqueurs are used sparingly. Cocktails vary widely across regions of the world. A written mention of the cocktail as a beverage appeared in the United States in 1803, and the first definition of a cocktail as an alcoholic beverage appeared in 1806. In 1862, Jerry Thomas published *How to Mix Drinks*, which included 10 cocktail recipes using bitters. With wine and [[Beer|beer]] less available during [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition]] (1920–1933), liquor-based cocktails became more popular. By 2023, the "cocktail in a can" was common in U.S. liquor stores.

French fashion designer and businesswoman, founder and namesake of the Chanel brand. Credited in the post–[[World War I|World War I]] era with popularizing a sporty, casual chic as the feminine standard of style, she extended her influence into jewelry, handbags and fragrance. Her signature scent, Chanel No. 5, became an iconic product, and her interlocked-CC monogram has been in use since the 1920s. Her couture house closed in 1939 at the outbreak of [[World War II]]. Chanel stayed in France during the German occupation and collaborated with the occupiers and the Vichy regime. According to declassified documents, she also collaborated directly with the Nazi intelligence service, the Sicherheitsdienst. After the war she was not charged as a collaborator, owing to intervention by her friend, British prime minister [[Winston Churchill|Winston Churchill]]. She returned to Paris in 1954 to revive her fashion house.

Dried, fully fermented seed of the cacao tree, *Theobroma cacao*. Its high fat content allows the bean to be ground into a [[Liquor|liquor]], from which cocoa butter and cocoa powder are extracted, and it is the basis of [[Chocolate|chocolate]]. The tree is native to the [[Amazon rainforest]], where it was first domesticated at least 5,300 years ago in South America. West Africa produces nearly 81% of the world's crop. In 2024, global production reached 5.8 million tonnes, with [[Ivory Coast]] leading at 38%.

Species of palm, *Cocos nucifera*, the only living species of the genus *Cocos* in the palm family (*Arecaceae*). The coconut tree provides food, fuel, cosmetics, folk medicine and building materials. Mature coconuts yield oil, coconut milk, charcoal from the hard shell and coir from the fibrous husk. Dried flesh is called copra. Originally native to Southeast Asia, New Guinea and the southwestern Pacific, the palm was domesticated by [[Austronesian peoples]] and spread during the [[Neolithic]] as far as the Pacific Islands and [[Madagascar]]. Trees can grow up to 30 meters tall and yield up to 75 fruits per year, though fewer than 30 is more typical. In 2024, world production of coconuts was 65.5 million tonnes, with 73% produced by [[Indonesia]], [[India]] and the [[Philippines]].

Giant terrestrial hermit crab, the largest living [[Arthropod|terrestrial arthropod]], also known as the robber crab. Adults can weigh up to 4.1 kg, with leg spans of up to 90 cm, and live on islands across the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Adults develop a tough abdominal exoskeleton, breathe through branchiostegal lungs and feed mainly on fallen fruit, nuts and seeds. Despite its name, [[Coconut|coconuts]] are not a significant part of its diet. The crab has been extirpated from most areas with large human populations, including mainland [[Australia]] and [[Madagascar]].

Australian external territory in the [[Indian Ocean]], approximately midway between [[Australia]] and Sri Lanka. It consists of two atolls with 27 coral islands, two of which are inhabited by around 600 people, mostly Cocos Malays who practice [[Sunni Islam]]. The islands were discovered in 1609 by William Keeling but not settled until the early 19th century. The Clunies-Ross family ruled them as a private fiefdom for almost 150 years. The British annexed the islands in 1857, and they were transferred to Australia in 1955.

Common name for several fish, chiefly the demersal genus *Gadus* in the family *Gadidae*. The two most common species are the Atlantic cod (*Gadus morhua*), which lives in colder waters across the [[Atlantic Ocean|North Atlantic]], and the Pacific cod (*Gadus macrocephalus*), found in both eastern and western regions of the northern Pacific. Cod has a mild flavor and dense, flaky, white flesh. Its livers are processed into cod liver oil, a common source of vitamin A, [[Vitamin D|vitamin D]], vitamin E and omega-3 fatty acids. Scrod is young Atlantic cod or [[Haddock|haddock]]. In the [[United Kingdom]], Atlantic cod is one of the most common ingredients in fish and chips. Severely shrunken Atlantic cod stocks have led to the marketing of other fish under culinary names of the form "x cod".

Babylonian legal text composed c. 1753 BC, one of the most recognizable legal texts from the ancient Near East. It is written in Old Babylonian Akkadian and purportedly by [[Hammurabi]], sixth king of the First Dynasty of [[Babylon]]. Its primary copy is inscribed on a stele 2.25 m tall, bearing about 4,130 lines of [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] text. The laws, which make up four fifths of the text, are casuistic "if ... then" sentences covering [[Criminal law|criminal]], family, [[Property law|property]] and commercial law. The stele was taken as plunder to [[Susa]] in present-day [[Iran]] and rediscovered in 1901; it now resides in the [[Louvre]]. Debate among Assyriologists has centered on its purpose, principles and relation to earlier law collections. Outside Assyriology, Hammurabi is regarded as an important figure in the history of law, and the document is treated as a true legal code.

Opiate and prodrug of morphine, mainly used to treat pain, coughing and diarrhea. It occurs naturally in the sap of the [[Opium|opium]] poppy, *Papaver somniferum*. Benefit may increase when it is combined with [[Paracetamol|paracetamol]] or a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug such as aspirin. The liver converts it into [[Morphine|morphine]]. Like other opioids, it carries risks of addiction and overdose. Discovered in 1832 by Pierre Jean Robiquet, it is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. In 2013, 249,000 kg was used, making it the most commonly taken opiate.

Largest surviving medieval illuminated manuscript, a Romanesque [[Latin]] Bible also known as the Devil's Bible for its full-page portrait of [[Satan]]. It was created in the early 13th century at the Benedictine monastery of Podlažice in Bohemia, now part of the [[Czech Republic]]. It contains the complete Bible in the [[Vulgate]] version, with encyclopedic and medical texts. The codex is 92 cm long and weighs 74.8 kg, with 310 leaves of vellum. Swedish forces seized it as war booty in 1648 during the [[Thirty Years' War]]; it is now in the National Library of Sweden in [[Stockholm]].

Manuscript book of pages bound along one edge, the historical ancestor of the modern book. Codices were usually made of [[Parchment|vellum]], parchment or [[Papyrus|papyrus]] rather than paper. Their gradual replacement of the [[Scroll|scroll]], the dominant document form of the ancient world, has been called the most important advance in bookmaking before the [[Printing press|printing press]]. The format was first described in the 1st century CE. By the 6th century the codex had completely replaced the scroll in the Christianized Greco-Roman world, as [[Christianity]] adopted it for the [[Bible]] and other texts.

Study of the properties of codes and their fitness for specific applications. Codes are used for [[Data compression|data compression]], [[Cryptography|cryptography]], error detection and correction, data transmission and data storage. The field draws on [[Information theory|information theory]], electrical engineering, mathematics, linguistics and [[Computer science|computer science]]. Data compression removes redundancy to transmit data more efficiently, while error correction adds redundancy to make transmission robust against disturbances. A typical music compact disc uses the Reed–Solomon code to correct scratches and dust. Claude Shannon developed information entropy as a measure of uncertainty in a message, essentially inventing information theory. Richard Hamming won the Turing Award in 1968 for his work at [[Bell Labs|Bell Labs]] on error-detecting and error-correcting codes. The binary Golay code, developed in 1949, can correct up to three errors in each 24-bit word and detect a fourth.

Statistical measure, denoted R² or r², of the proportion of variation in a dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variable or variables. In simple [[Linear regression|linear regression]], it equals the square of the [[Correlation|correlation coefficient]]. It is always smaller than 1 and usually greater than 0, though it can be negative when the mean of the data fits the outcomes better than the model. Unlike error measures such as RMSE, which have arbitrary ranges, it can be expressed as a percentage.

Ancient group of lobe-finned fishes in the class *Actinistia*, more closely related to [[Lungfish|lungfish]] and [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]] than to ray-finned fish. Fossils date from the Devonian period, more than 410 million years ago. Coelacanths were thought to have become extinct at the end of the [[Cretaceous]], around 66 million years ago. The first living species, *Latimeria chalumnae*, was described from specimens caught off [[South Africa]] from 1938 onward. It is also known from the seas around the [[Comoros|Comoro Islands]]. The Indonesian coelacanth, *Latimeria menadoensis*, was discovered in the late 1990s. Its reappearance more than 60 million years after its supposed extinction makes it the best-known example of a Lazarus taxon. Fossil coelacanths show body shapes more diverse than previously thought.

Extinct genus of small, ground-dwelling theropod [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]] from the late [[Triassic]] period, found in what is now the southwestern United States. It was a slender bipedal [[Carnivore|carnivore]] that could grow up to 3 m long. Edward Drinker Cope described the genus in 1889 from remains collected in [[New Mexico]]. One of the earliest known dinosaur genera, it is also one of the most specimen-rich.

American filmmaking duo, Joel and Ethan Coen. Their films span many genres and styles. Acclaimed works include *Blood Simple* (1984), *Fargo* (1996), *The Big Lebowski* (1998), *No Country for Old Men* (2007) and *A Serious Man* (2009). The brothers generally write, direct and produce their films jointly, and they have shared editing credits under the alias Roderick Jaynes. *Fargo* won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Original Screenplay, and *No Country for Old Men* won Best Picture, Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay. *Barton Fink* won the Palme d'Or.

Field of study in [[Neuroscience|neuroscience]] and [[Psychology|psychology]] concerned with a child's development in information processing, conceptual resources, perception and language learning. It is often described in four components: reasoning, intelligence, language and memory, which begin to develop in early infancy. [[Jean Piaget|Jean Piaget]] was a major force in establishing the field, proposing four stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational. Many of his theoretical claims have since fallen out of favor, though his description of age-related changes in cognition is still broadly accepted. Alternative models include information-processing theory and Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory. Nature versus nurture is now widely regarded as a false dichotomy, because gene activity interacts with experience from the earliest points in development.

Mental phenomenon in which people hold fundamentally conflicting [[Belief|beliefs]], attitudes or behaviors. The resulting psychological discomfort motivates a person to change a belief, explain something away or take action that reduces the inconsistency. [[Leon Festinger|Leon Festinger]] proposed the theory in *A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance* (1957), arguing that people strive for internal consistency. People may reduce dissonance through rationalization, selective perception or avoidance of contradictory information. Festinger's theory remains one of the most influential in [[Social psychology|social psychology]].

Subdiscipline of psychology that studies human mental processes such as [[Attention|attention]], language use, [[Memory|memory]], perception, problem solving, creativity and reasoning. It originated in the 1960s as a break from [[Behaviorism|behaviorism]], which had held from the 1920s to 1950s that unobservable mental processes lay outside empirical science. Researchers in [[Linguistics|linguistics]], [[Cybernetics|cybernetics]] and applied psychology had used models of mental processing to explain behavior. Wartime needs in [[World War II|World War II]] led Donald Broadbent to integrate human-performance research with [[Information theory|information theory]]. Allen Newell and Herbert Simon developed the concept of [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] and later collaborated with cognitive psychologists. Work derived from the field has since been integrated into cognitive science, linguistics and economics.

Living arrangement in which unmarried people live together as a couple, often in a long-term or permanent intimate relationship. Such arrangements have become increasingly common in [[Western world|Western countries]] since the late 20th century. The trend began in [[Scandinavia]], and in Mediterranean Europe cohabitation rose after the mid-1990s. In [[Portugal]], most children have been born to unwed parents since 2015, constituting 60% of the total in 2021. Christian doctrine has traditionally opposed unmarried cohabitation, but some denominations now view it as a precursor to [[Marriage|marriage]]. Cited factors include women's workforce participation, contraception, secularization and changing views on sexuality.
